    At Cypher 2026, our CEO & Co-founder Sravanth Aluru sat down to talk about where AI video is heading, and why it’s about much more than generating clips. A few takeaways from the conversation: 1️⃣ Video is a step toward multimodal intelligence. The bigger opportunity is AI that understands the world through vision, voice, and eventually 3D, laying the groundwork for AI + robotics. India needs sovereign multimodal capabilities to lead here. 2️⃣ Short-form is where the action is today. The frontier is ready for short clips and ~1-minute videos, which opens up a huge market beyond filmmaking: product ads, educational videos, devotional storytelling, and even replacing pamphlets with video. 3️⃣ Lower cost means new creators. By bringing down the cost of access, Varya is reaching businesses and creators who couldn’t afford frontier video models before. 4️⃣ Built for India’s nuances. With support from the IndiaAI Mission, we built proprietary datasets rather than relying on others’ IP, so our models understand cultural details, like the difference between a kurti and a saree. 5️⃣ What’s next: Varya 2.0. Varya 1.0 matched the global open frontier at a significantly lower cost. Varya 2.0 aims to close the gap with closed frontier models while staying efficient. A lot is cooking in the labs.     Everyone is talking about using AI to work faster. But are we actually making people better at their jobs, or just more dependent on AI? I was watching a conversation between Raj Shamani and Sravanth Aluru, CEO of Avataar, and one part really stood out. Raj Shamani had an idea during the conversation that he wanted to implement immediately: an AI Chief of Staff. Think about how companies operate today. Employees spend hours preparing reports, updating dashboards, chasing information across departments, and putting together documents for someone else to review. What if AI agents handled most of that preparation? Imagine an AI agent that understands your company's internal knowledge, connects data across different systems, prepares reports, identifies what needs attention, and routes decisions to the right people. Instead of asking an employee to spend hours preparing a document, AI prepares it, and the employee focuses on identifying the three things that actually matter. Or instead of a manager opening five dashboards to understand why transactions are failing, an AI agent connects the data, identifies patterns, and recommends what needs to be done. We're moving from dashboards that tell us what happened to AI agents that help us decide what to do next. But this also raises an interesting question about AI dependency. If AI starts doing all the analysis, preparation, and coordination, are employees becoming more capable or simply more reliant on it? I think the distinction comes down to where we keep human involvement. AI should handle the repetitive work of gathering and connecting information. People should still own the judgment, challenge the recommendations, and make the decisions. Maybe the real opportunity isn't giving every employee access to ChatGPT. It's redesigning how companies operate so that AI agents handle the groundwork and employees spend more time on work that actually requires their expertise.     Sravanth Aluru, CEO and Co-Founder of Avataar, took the Cypher 2026 stage with his keynote session, “AI Reads the Manual. Your Company Never Wrote One.” While 80% of executives say AI makes them more productive, Sravanth noted, only 6% of organisations see more than a 5% earnings impact. The reason, he said, is that companies have never written down their know-how in a way AI can use. Small gaps also compound fast: a model that is 97% accurate on each step succeeds only 36% of the time across a 34-step workflow. His answer is an AI-native operating model built on a unified ontology, persistent organisational memory and governance. Distilled small language models then handle most of the volume at a fraction of frontier costs. The winners of the next decade, he argued, will be the organisations that learn the fastest. Thank you, Sravanth, for giving the room a blueprint for writing that manual.     I gave one of my most important teams AI to use for everything, and a few months later they were worse at their jobs. I’d pushed them to use it for about six months. What I noticed was that they slowly became dependent on it. They stopped making their own calls and let the AI do the thinking, and the original ideas I used to get from them stopped coming. My best people weren’t producing the way they used to. I’ve always believed that a bit of messy, imperfect human thinking, which has an element of stupidity, is where original ideas come from, and that side had disappeared. So in our recent episode, I asked Sravanth Aluru, CEO & Co-founder of Avataar, how you put AI across a whole company without people's thinking getting worse. He pointed out that there’s research showing this dependency. A 2025 study from MIT’s Media Lab measured people’s brain activity while they wrote, some using ChatGPT, some on their own. The ones leaning on AI showed the weakest brain activity, could barely remember what they’d just written, and stayed less engaged even afterwards, once the AI was taken away. His fix comes down to one change. The problem, he said, is letting people use AI as a tool to do their work, because the moment someone hands their thinking over to it, they start getting weaker. So turn it around. Let the AI do the grunt work on its own, and bring people in only for the parts that need human judgment, the decisions with stakes and no clean answer. The way he put it, the AI should be the one pulling people in, handing them the calls only a human can make. People stay the ones making the decisions that matter, and that keeps them sharp. So how do you set this up, in a company or in your own work? Watch the full conversation to learn more: https://lnkd.in/ghXpGJCx #rajshamani #figuringout
